'''Elly Margaret Tanaka''', {{postnominal-GBR|FRS}} (born in [[Boston]], Massachusetts, in 1965)<ref>{{cite news |last=Sica |first=Julia |title=Elly Tanaka, die Herrin der Axolotl, wird Chefin des Instituts für molekulare Biotechnologie |url=https://www.derstandard.at/story/3000000211622/elly-tanaka-die-herrin-der-axolotl-wird-chefin-des-instituts-fuer-molekulare-biotechnologie |work=Der Standard |date=14 March 2024 |language=de}}</ref> is an American-Austrian<ref name="TanakaOutreach">{{cite web |title=The full breath of society: Elly Tanaka on outreach and science communications |url=https://www.oeaw.ac.at/en/news/das-volle-spektrum-der-gesellschaft-elly-tanaka-ueber-outreach-und-wissenschaftskommunikation |publisher=Austrian Academy of Sciences |date=1 October 2026 |language=de |access-date=12 November 2026}}</ref> [[biochemist]] and Scientific Director at the [[Institute of Molecular Biotechnology]] of the Austrian Academy of Sciences (IMBA) at the [[Vienna Biocenter]], Austria. Tanaka studies the molecular cell biology of limb and spinal cord [[Regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] in salamanders and other systems as well as the [[evolution]] of regeneration.

==Early life and education==

Tanaka was born in Boston (Massachusetts), and obtained a bachelor's degree in biochemistry from [[Harvard University]] in 1987 and a PhD from the [[University of California, San Francisco]] in 1993, where she had worked in the lab of [[Marc W. Kirschner]].<ref name="library.cshl.edu">{{Cite web|title=Oral History {{!}} Elly Tanaka|url=http://library.cshl.edu/oralhistory/speaker/elly-tanaka/|access-date=16 August 2020|website=library.cshl.edu|archive-date=3 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211203192203/http://library.cshl.edu/oralhistory/speaker/elly-tanaka/|url-status=live}}</ref> She then became a postdoctoral researcher in the lab of [[Jeremy Brockes]] at [[University College London]] and  Ludwig Institute.<ref name="library.cshl.edu" /> 

== Scientific career ==
Tanaka started her own lab at the [[Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics]] (MPI-CBG) in [[Dresden]] (Germany) in 1999.<ref name="library.cshl.edu" /> In 2008, she became a professor at the Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden (CRTD) of the [[Technische Universität Dresden]].<ref name="library.cshl.edu" /> She became director of the center in 2014,<ref name="cv">{{cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Tanaka_Elly/CV|title=Academy of Europe: CV|publisher=[[Academia Europaea]]|access-date=21 March 2020|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927155214/http://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Tanaka_Elly/CV |archive-date=27 September 2017 }}</ref> before becoming senior scientist at the Research Institute of Molecular Pathology (IMP) in Vienna in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imp.ac.at/news/detail/article/press-release-elly-tanaka-joins-the-imp-as-senior-scientist/|title=Press Release: Elly Tanaka joins the IMP as Senior Scientist|publisher=The Research Institute of Molecular Pathology|access-date=21 March 2020|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927155133/https://www.imp.ac.at/news/detail/article/press-release-elly-tanaka-joins-the-imp-as-senior-scientist/|archive-date=27 September 2017}}</ref> In 2024, Tanaka joined the Institute of Molecular Biotechnology of the Austrian Academy of Sciences (IMBA) as Scientific Director.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.oeaw.ac.at/imba/research-highlights/news/elly-tanaka-imbas-new-scientific-director/|title=Press Release: Elly Tanaka: IMBA's new Scientific Director|publisher=Institute of Molecular Biotechnology|access-date=14 March 2024}}</ref>

== Research ==

Tanaka studies the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable salamanders to regenerate complex tissues, using the [[axolotl]] (''Ambystoma mexicanum'') as her principal model organism.<ref name="FWF">{{cite web |title=The Axolotl and the Mystery of Regeneration |url=https://www.fwf.ac.at/en/discover/discoveries/elly-tanaka |website=Austrian Science Fund (FWF)}}</ref> Her laboratory developed methods for fluorescent cell labelling, live imaging, transgenesis and genome editing in the axolotl, enabling researchers to trace the origins and behaviour of cells during regeneration and investigate the functions of individual genes.<ref name="Khattak2013">{{cite journal |vauthors=Khattak S, Schuez M, Richter T, Knapp D, Haigo SL, Sandoval-Guzmán T, Hradlikova K, Duemmler A, Kerney R, Tanaka EM |title=Germline transgenic methods for tracking cells and testing gene function during regeneration in the axolotl |journal=Stem Cell Reports |year=2013 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=90–103 |doi=10.1016/j.stemcr.2013.03.002 |pmid=24052945 |pmc=3757742 }}</ref><ref name="Currie2016">{{cite journal |vauthors=Currie JD, Kawaguchi A, Traspas RM, Schuez M, Chara O, Tanaka EM |title=Live Imaging of Axolotl Digit Regeneration Reveals Spatiotemporal Choreography of Diverse Connective Tissue Progenitor Pools |journal=Developmental Cell |year=2016 |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=411–423 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2016.10.013 |pmid=27840105 |pmc=5127896 }}</ref><ref name="Fei2018">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fei JF, Lou WP, Knapp D, Murawala P, Gerber T, Taniguchi Y, Nowoshilow S, Khattak S, Tanaka EM |title=Application and optimization of CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome engineering in axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) |journal=Nature Protocols |year=2018 |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=2908–2943 |doi=10.1038/s41596-018-0071-0 |pmid=30429597 |hdl=21.11116/0000-0002-AA54-0 }}</ref> Together with collaborators, her group sequenced and annotated the axolotl genome, published in 2018, providing a resource for investigating the genetic regulation of regeneration.<ref name="Nowoshilow2018">{{cite journal |last1=Nowoshilow |first1=S. |last2=Schloissnig |first2=S. |last3=Fei |first3=J. F. |last4=Dahl |first4=A. |last5=Pang |first5=A. W. C. |last6=Pippel |first6=M. |last7=Winkler |first7=S. |last8=Hastie |first8=A. R. |last9=Young |first9=G. |last10=Roscito |first10=J. G. |last11=Falcon |first11=F. |last12=Knapp |first12=D. |last13=Powell |first13=S. |last14=Cruz |first14=A. |last15=Cao |first15=H. |last16=Habermann |first16=B. |last17=Hiller |first17=M. |last18=Tanaka |first18=E. M. |last19=Myers |first19=E. W. |title=The axolotl genome and the evolution of key tissue formation regulators |journal=Nature |year=2018 |volume=554 |issue=7690 |pages=50–55 |doi=10.1038/nature25458 |pmid=29364872 |bibcode=2018Natur.554...50N }}</ref>

A central contribution of Tanaka's research has been to establish the cellular origins of regenerated limbs. In 2009, her group showed that cells contributing to the [[blastema]]—the population of progenitor cells that forms at an amputation site—largely retain restrictions on the types of tissue they can produce, rather than reverting to a universally pluripotent state.<ref name="Kragl2009">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kragl M, Knapp D, Nacu E, Khattak S, Maden M, Epperlein HH, Tanaka EM |title=Cells keep a memory of their tissue origin during axolotl limb regeneration |journal=Nature |year=2009 |volume=460 |issue=7251 |pages=60–65 |doi=10.1038/nature08152 |pmid=19571878 |bibcode=2009Natur.460...60K }}</ref> In 2018, her team demonstrated that connective tissue cells called [[fibroblast]]s lose their specialised characteristics and give rise to progenitor cells during limb regeneration. This established that these regenerative cells arise from differentiated tissue rather than a reserve of dedicated stem cells.<ref name="Gerber2018">{{cite journal |vauthors=Gerber T, Murawala P, Knapp D, Masselink W, Schuez M, Hermann S, Gac-Santel M, Nowoshilow S, Kageyama J, Khattak S, Currie JD, Camp JG, Tanaka EM, Treutlein B |title=Single-cell analysis uncovers convergence of cell identities during axolotl limb regeneration |journal=Science |year=2018 |volume=362 |issue=6413 |article-number=eaaq0681 |doi=10.1126/science.aaq0681 |pmid=30262634 |pmc=6669047 |bibcode=2018Sci...362..681G }}</ref> Comparisons with frogs, which cannot regenerate complete limbs as adults, linked their limited regenerative capacity to incomplete fibroblast dedifferentiation.<ref name="Lin2021">{{cite journal |vauthors=Lin TY, Gerber T, Taniguchi-Sugiura Y, Murawala P, Hermann S, Grosser L, Shibata E, Treutlein B, Tanaka EM |title=Fibroblast dedifferentiation as a determinant of successful regeneration |journal=Developmental Cell |year=2021 |volume=56 |issue=10 |pages=1541–1551.e6 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2021.04.016 |pmid=34004152 |pmc=8140481 }}</ref>

Tanaka's group also investigated how cells retain information about their position within a limb and use it to reconstruct missing structures. In 2024, the team showed that connective tissue cells at different limb positions have distinct [[chromatin]] states, providing an epigenetic basis for positional information.<ref name="Kawaguchi2024">{{cite journal |last1=Kawaguchi |first1=A. |last2=Wang |first2=J. |last3=Knapp |first3=D. |last4=Murawala |first4=P. |last5=Nowoshilow |first5=S. |last6=Masselink |first6=W. |last7=Taniguchi-Sugiura |first7=Y. |last8=Fei |first8=J. F. |last9=Tanaka |first9=E. M. |title=A chromatin code for limb segment identity in axolotl limb regeneration |journal=Developmental Cell |year=2024 |volume=59 |issue=16 |pages=2239–2253.e9 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2024.05.002 |pmid=38788714}}</ref> In 2025, her group identified a role for the transcription factor ''[[HAND2|Hand2]]'' in maintaining positional memory along the limb's thumb-to-little-finger axis. Its persistent activity in posterior connective tissue cells before injury helps organise the signals that pattern the regenerating limb.<ref name="Otsuki2025">{{cite journal |vauthors=Otsuki L, Plattner SA, Taniguchi-Sugiura Y, Falcon F, Tanaka EM |title=Molecular basis of positional memory in limb regeneration |journal=Nature |year=2025 |volume=642 |issue=8068 |pages=730–738 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09036-5 |pmid=40399677 |pmc=12176643 |bibcode=2025Natur.642..730O }}</ref>

Beyond limb regeneration, Tanaka's research encompasses the spinal cord, brain, heart and retina.<ref name="FWF" /> Her laboratory has shown that axolotl heart muscle cells resume division following injury<ref name="FWF" /> and is investigating how neuronal circuits are rebuilt during brain regeneration.<ref name="Lust2022">{{cite journal |vauthors=Lust K, Maynard A, Gomes T |display-authors=etal |title=Single-cell analyses of axolotl telencephalon organization, neurogenesis, and regeneration |journal=Science |year=2022 |volume=377 |issue=6610 |article-number=eabp9262 |doi=10.1126/science.abp9262 |pmid=36048956 }}</ref> The group has also generated [[retinal pigment epithelium]] from human embryonic stem cells to investigate potential approaches to repairing retinal damage.<ref name="Zhu2013">{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhu Y, Carido M, Meinhardt A, Kurth T, Karl MO, Ader M, Tanaka EM |title=Three-dimensional neuroepithelial culture from human embryonic stem cells and its use for quantitative conversion to retinal pigment epithelium |journal=PLOS ONE |year=2013 |volume=8 |issue=1 |article-number=e54552 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0054552 |doi-access=free |pmid=23358448 |pmc=3554725 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...854552Z }}</ref><ref name="Schreiter2020">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schreiter S, Vafia K, Barsacchi R |display-authors=etal |title=A Human Retinal Pigment Epithelium-Based Screening Platform Reveals Inducers of Photoreceptor Outer Segments Phagocytosis |journal=Stem Cell Reports |year=2020 |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=1347–1361 |doi=10.1016/j.stemcr.2020.10.013 |pmid=33242397 |pmc=7724476 }}</ref>

== Science communication and public engagement ==
Tanaka advocates public engagement as a responsibility of publicly funded researchers, a contribution to societal debate and a way for scientists to broaden communication skills.<ref name="TanakaOutreach"></ref> She has supported IMBA outreach, including school workshops, science festivals and programmes for disadvantaged children.<ref name="TanakaOutreach" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Outreach & Dialogue |url=https://www.oeaw.ac.at/imba/about-imba/outreach-dialogue |publisher=Institute of Molecular Biotechnology |access-date=12 November 2026}}</ref> Tanaka uses axolotl regeneration to explain basic research and its potential medical relevance, and frequently appears in Austrian and international media.<ref name="TanakaOutreach" /> She has also called for a national science communication strategy in Austria to reach diverse audiences.<ref name="TanakaOutreach" />
